Statement to the Court on Behalf of the Victims of Harold J. Nicholson's Espionage is declassified CIA document 0000104909, dated May 1, 1997 in the catalog. The sample is a letter dated June 2, 1997, to Judge James Cacheris in Alexandria, Virginia. The writer signs as Acting Director of Central Intelligence.

The letter says Nicholson betrayed his friends and colleagues and put their lives in danger. He revealed, or planned to reveal, the names and posts of many CIA officers working in secret. Some could no longer do the assignments they were trained for. Officers under the deepest cover were withdrawn, their missions and lives at risk.

cia-0000117909: Recent Developments in Southeastern Europe is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000117909, dated June 6, 1950. cia-0000119209:
This March 1984 CIA document reports Vietnam's assessment of American policy in its region. The heading adds that Hanoi kept a continuing hope for something from the United States, then breaks off before naming it. Nearly a decade after the war ended, the two countries still had no normal relations.

Hearing the other side's view was the point of such reporting. The document sets out how Vietnamese leaders read Washington's moves and what they still wanted from America. It captures a frozen relationship beginning, very slowly, to thaw, and it shows the agency listening to a former enemy whose choices still shaped Southeast Asia.
cia-0000119709:
A February 1954 CIA paper forecasts probable developments in Argentina. President Peron's second term was running into economic trouble, and his grip on the country was weakening. Eighteen months later the military would drive him from power.

The paper weighs the forces pressing on Peron's government and the paths the country might take. Argentina mattered to Washington as South America's second great power and as a test of populist rule. Reading the forecast now, one can judge how clearly the agency saw the fall coming. It is a period piece from the years when Peronism first rose, broke, and began its long afterlife.
cia-0000124309: Dated April 1951, this CIA document carries two items: the arrival of American prisoners of war in Canton, and their transfer onward, the heading breaking off. The paired items trace the men's movement step by step through Chinese hands during the Korean War. Paired items of arrival and transfer sketch the route men took into the interior, the same route later tracing work would follow in reverse for decades.
cia-0000132209: Situation report 526, from January 1991, notes the European Community boosting aid to frontline states. Those states bore heavy costs from the war on their borders, and European money helped hold the coalition's Arab members steady. The report records the aid decision. Aid to frontline states was coalition maintenance in cash form, paying the neighbors of Iraq and Kuwait to bear refugee, trade, and military burdens without wavering.
cia-0000132409: The situation in Cuba fills a CIA document dated February 1, 1959. It was filed just one month after Castro's victory, which makes it one of the earliest Cuba files in the set. The revolution was only weeks old at that point. Washington was still deciding what the change of power meant, and the document gives the situation as analysts first found it.
cia-0000132509: Chile treating Cuba as a bilateral problem for the United States fills a CIA document dated February 2, 1961. Santiago wanted no part of a joint campaign against Havana. Chile's stance pointed ahead to the split that would open inside the Organization of American States over Cuba. The short document notes the position and what it meant for Washington's hopes of regional unity.
cia-0000135909: A meeting record in the declassified CIA files, dated 4 May 1954, covers points covered in talks held on the first and second of June, the speaker's name deleted. The record comes from the run-up to the June 1954 coup that removed President Arbenz, the goal of the CIA plan called PBSUCCESS. Small as it is, the sheet documents one task, one report, or one order inside a much larger secret effort.
cia-0000136209: The open CIA files hold a press file dated 1 May 1954 that deals with the Guatemala press file for the eighth through the eleventh of June. The record comes from the run-up to the June 1954 coup that removed President Arbenz, the goal of the CIA plan called PBSUCCESS. cia-0000136309: Operational Situation Report No. 12, dated late June 1954, tracks PBSUCCESS rebel teams across eastern Guatemala. It reports the combined Johnny-Danny force capturing Chiquimula except the enemy barracks, after a requested air strike failed when both F-47s had mechanical trouble. Other teams report no change, request mortars and 20-mm guns, or stay silent without radios. A resupply flight could not locate its team near Gualan. The report shows an invasion running on patchy information.
cia-0000137009: Communists in embassies are violating asylum, the themes in this June 1954 cable charge. Asyleed communists pass arms and money in and out by radio. They conduct propaganda from inside. Carlos Manuel Pellecer sits in the Mexican embassy. He is said to be making tape recordings. The tapes aid subversive propaganda by party remnants. Themes to push are listed. The government is as democratic and just as possible. There are no blood baths. Asyleed communists and common criminals grossly violate asylum's privilege.
un-sc-res-1309: One entry in the Council's numbered series is Resolution 1309, catalogued for 2000 by this library. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-1409: Resolution 1409 of the Security Council reaches readers here as an official record text, catalogued under the year 2002. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades.
un-sc-res-1509:
In September 2003 the Security Council passed Resolution 1509, creating the United Nations Mission in Liberia, known as UNMIL. Liberia's long civil war had just ended with a peace deal and Charles Taylor's exile. The Council sent a large peacekeeping force to hold the calm.

The text sets out what the mission could do, from guarding the ceasefire to helping disarm fighters and protect civilians. It also covers support for elections and rebuilding state authority across the country. The resolution marks the moment Liberia's recovery became a shared world project, led on the ground by UN troops.
un-sc-res-1609: Under number 1609, the Council placed another formal decision in its record, and this collection keeps the record text via Wikisource. The preamble does the persuading, citing history and principle; the operative part does the governing. Students of the institution read both halves together, and this entry preserves them together, in order, as voted.
un-sc-res-1709: Security Council Resolution 1709, adopted in 2006, is held here in its official-record wording via Wikisource. The Council produces hundreds of pages of such text in a busy year, each piece voted and numbered. This piece is preserved entire, so its place in the year's business can be judged from the document itself.
cia-0000135709: Brigade 2506's Spanish archive holds this document, dated 6 February 1961. By February the exile force was in its final training phase, weeks from embarkation. plos-pone-0000009:
Pamela Colosimo and Nicholas Tolwinski reported in 2006 on how a fruit fly embryo gives its cells a sense of direction. Planar polarity is the orderly alignment of cells across a sheet of tissue, like hairs all pointing one way. In the Drosophila embryo, that alignment is set up early and guides later growth.

Three players share the credit in their results: the Wnt signal, the Hedgehog signal, and a junction protein, Armadillo, also known as beta-catenin. Together they establish polarity across the embryo's surface. frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d109: Ambassador Harriman wrote to Roosevelt from Moscow on November 9, 1943, his second dispatch in three days in this series. frus-1945-malta-yalta-d109:

Swami Vivekananda, the Hindu monk who addressed the Chicago Parliament of Religions in 1893, gave the lectures printed as Raja Yoga in 1896. They teach the yoga of mind control, based on Patanjali's old Yoga Sutras. The book carried yoga thought to American readers.

crowley-777-1909:

crowley-equinox-vol-1-no-09:

fort-outcast-manufacturers-1909:

hodgson-ghost-pirates-1909:
Sailors fear their own ship in William Hope Hodgson's novel The Ghost Pirates, from 1909. Strange shapes climb from the sea at dusk. Gear fails, men die, and a dark shape looms past the hull. The crew must face what hunts them.

Hodgson builds fear slow, watch by watch, night by night. His years at sea make each task and term feel true. The end is stark and sad. Many rank it as the best tale of a cursed ship in weird prose. petrie-arts-crafts-ancient-egypt-1909:
W. M. Flinders Petrie shows how Egypt made its goods in The Arts and Crafts of Ancient Egypt, out in 1909. Stone work, glaze, glass, wood, and metal each get a part. Petrie had dug up the shops and tools in his years on site. He tells how each craft grew, what tools it used, and how fine its best work could be.

His eye for how a thing was made sets the book apart. Fine ware and rough ware both get fair words. The book is a shop tour of a lost world. Crafts folk still learn from it.
lodge-survival-of-man-1909:
Oliver Lodge, a chief of the science of waves and wires, made his case for life past death in The Survival of Man, out in 1909. Lodge held high posts in the schools of Britain. He turned their tools on the dark room: notes, tests, and checks for fraud, weighed with a calm, fair hand through years of sittings.

He claims some notes from the dead pass all fair tests. His rank gave the claim a weight no mere fan could match. The book took the theme to the heart of science. Its calm tone is its force.
carrington-eusapia-palladino-1909:
Hereward Carrington tests a famed seer at close range in Eusapia Palladino and Her Phenomena, out in 1909. Palladino was a stout dame from Naples whose sittings shook the age. Tables rose, hands grasped guests, and strange stuff seemed to flow from her frame. Carrington sat through long runs of tests in Naples with peers from the chief band for such study.

He grants fraud in part, yet holds a strange rest stands. His tale is tense, fair, and full of night by night notes. The book is the best close tale of the most fought seer.
stewart-origin-of-the-werewolf-superstit:
Caroline Taylor Stewart hunts the roots of a belief in The Origin of the Werewolf Superstition, her study of 1909. Stewart was a sage of tongues at a school in the United States. She traces the wolf man from old Greek tales and Rome's verse through wolf cults, trials, and tales of the north. Each age, she shows, bent the beast to its own fears and faiths.

Her tone is calm and learned, free of thrills. She treats the theme as a thread in man's tale, not a freak. The book is the base on which new study of the theme stands.
bogoras-chukchee-1904-1909:
Waldemar Bogoras spent years among the Chukchi people of far northeast Siberia, and this large study came out in 1909. His work formed part of the Jesup work in the North Pacific. The texts were set down word for word as they were told to him. He lived with the people he wrote about and learned their tongue. He also made long trips by sled and boat along the coast.

The pages cover daily life, kin ties, tales, and rites in close detail. A long share deals with shamans, spirits, and the cures and songs they used. It stays a key firsthand source for the folk ways of the Chukchi.
davies-mythology-british-druids-1809:
Edward Davies, a Welsh cleric, set out his grand scheme of British druid lore in this book of 1809. He wrote in the Romantic age, when old British roots drew much public zeal. His aim was to trace the druids back to the dawn of faith.

Davies tied the druids to Noah, the flood, and the ark of the Bible. He read old Welsh verse and stone works as proof of one vast rite scheme. Grand and flawed, the book fixed what druidism meant for a whole age of readers. Few books show the age's hunger for old roots so well.
lodge-ether-of-space-1909:
Oliver Lodge, an English physicist, gave the ether its last great public defense in this book of 1909. He wrote for lay readers, in clear and warm terms. By then the new work of Einstein had made the ether look like a needless prop.

Lodge sets out what the ether does in his scheme, from light to the pull of worlds. He holds that space must be full of a real stuff that bears all waves and forces. The book shows the old view at its peak, just as its age came to a close.
lorentz-theory-of-electrons-1909:
Hendrik Antoon Lorentz, a Dutch sage, gave these talks at Columbia in New York, and they came out in book form in 1909. His theme is the electron, the tiny charged part he had helped to place at the heart of physics. The talks sum up his life's work.

Lorentz shows how swarms of electrons can give light, heat rays, and the split hues of the Zeeman effect. He sets out the shrink of fast bodies that bears his name, tied to a still ether. The book is the old scheme in its last strict, fine form, by its chief maker.
macauliffe-sikh-religion-vol1-1909:

Nanak's travels, hymns, and talks with Hindus and Muslims fill these pages. Macauliffe aimed to let Sikh texts speak in their own voice, not through hostile reports. He quotes the hymns at length and adds notes on custom and belief. The whole set still stands as a base text for the study of Sikhism.
macauliffe-sikh-religion-vol2-1909:

Four Gurus lead this book: Angad, Amar Das, Ram Das, and the years between them. Their hymns come with tales of how each man held the young faith firm. New towns, new rites, and a growing flock mark the age. Readers see how a small group became a lasting faith.
macauliffe-sikh-religion-vol3-1909:

Arjan drew the hymns of the first Gurus and of holy men into one book, the Granth. Macauliffe gives long extracts in English and tells how the work was done. Arjan's death at the hands of the Mughal state closes the tale. The book shows the faith gaining a scripture and a martyr.
macauliffe-sikh-religion-vol4-1909:

macauliffe-sikh-religion-vol5-1909:

Pages tell of Gobind Singh's wars, his court of poets, and his loss of his sons. In 1708 he named the Granth, the holy book, as Guru after him. Macauliffe gives the Guru's own hymns in English with the tales round them. The human line of Gurus ends here in high drama.
macauliffe-sikh-religion-vol6-1909:

Hymns of the Gurus stand beside songs of the Bhagats, holy men from Hindu and Muslim paths. Long notes explain hard lines, old words, and points of faith. Macauliffe also sums up what sets Sikh belief apart. The book closes the first full English account of Sikhism.
shahnameh-warner-vol4-1909:

Arab conquest closes the age of the shahs in these last tales. Kings look back on lost glory and warn those who come next. The poem ends in a tone of loss and pride. The full set still serves readers who want the whole epic in English.
heindel-rosicrucian-cosmo-conception-190:

Worlds form and fade in vast rounds of time in his scheme. Man's dense body, life body, and mind each take form in turn. Death, birth anew, and the law of cause fill the mid part. The book ends with steps for the soul's growth toward full sight.
angela-foligno-divine-consolation-1909:
Angela of Foligno told her Book of Divine Consolation to her priest. Mary G. Steegmann gave the work English dress in 1909. Angela was a rich wife in Umbria who lost her kin and turned to God. She joined the third order of St. Francis in her grief.

marx-capital-vol-3-1909:

shakespeare-sonnets-1609:

london-martin-eden-1909:
Jack London published Martin Eden in 1909, his tragic Künstlerroman of a working-class sailor who educates himself. A sailor educates himself into a famous writer, then discovers success is hollow, in London's most bitter novel. He protested that Eden was an individualist, not a socialist, and that the book indicted Eden's creed, not society's alone.

nietzsche-zarathustra-common-1909:

nietzsche-beyond-good-evil-zimmern-1909:
Friedrich Nietzsche published Beyond Good and Evil in 1886, a sharp attack on the philosophy and morals of his age. The English text here is Helen Zimmern's translation of 1909. james-meaning-truth-1909:

He clarifies how ideas lead us from one part of experience to another. The essays also revisit radical empiricism, his view that relations are as real as things. bateson-mendel-principles-1909:
William Bateson was a Cambridge biologist who became the loudest English champion of Gregor Mendel's newly rediscovered laws of inheritance. He shows how traits in peas, poultry, and other bred stock split and recombine in fixed ratios across generations. He defends Mendel's rules against older ideas of blending inheritance with case after case. The book sold Mendelism to the English-speaking world and trained its first geneticists. soddy-interpretation-radium-1909:
Frederick Soddy was a British chemist who worked with Rutherford on how atoms break apart. His 1909 book The Interpretation of Radium explains radioactivity to general readers with patience and flair. Radium was then a wonder substance, glowing in the dark and defying old chemistry.

Soddy shows that atoms of heavy elements decay step by step, throwing off rays and vast stored energy. He grasps early that this energy, if freed, could power cities or destroy them. tyrrell-christianity-cross-roads-1909:
George Tyrrell was an Irish Jesuit whose doubts about scholastic theology led to his expulsion from his order and excommunication. His Christianity at the Cross-Roads appeared in 1909, the year of his death. The posthumous book calls for a living, developing Catholicism.

Tyrrell argues that the church must choose between treating its formulas as final cages and treating them as signs of a living experience. He looks to a future synthesis in which faith and modern knowledge correct each other. Modernist readers claimed the book as their testament, while Rome's condemnation gave it a martyr's fame.
fillmore-christian-healing-1909:

Fillmore reads the Bible as a map of the soul, with its persons and places standing for states of mind. Health, he teaches, follows when thought aligns with the divine life already within the body. khunrath-amphitheatrum-sapientiae-1609:
Heinrich Khunrath was a German physician and Hermetic philosopher whose Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae appeared in 1609. The title means Amphitheater of Eternal Wisdom, and the book is built like its title: a theater of engraved visions. It is the great Christian-kabbalistic alchemical emblem book.

Nine large engravings show the alchemist at prayer and at the furnace, angels, gates, and the stone as Christ-like figures of renewal. Khunrath joins laboratory work to devotion, holding that the adept must be reborn along with his matter. Collectors prize the plates, and scholars mine the book for the period's union of faith and furnace.
shahnama-warner-vol-4-1909:

In this volume the heroic age rolls on, with champions whose strength and pride drive the tale. Court intrigue, single combat, and tragic error shape the action, as they do throughout the poem. The Warners kept close to the Persian while making the story readable. Readers who follow the set volume by volume watch a whole civilization's memory of itself pass in review.
kepler-astronomia-nova-1609:
Johannes Kepler published Astronomia Nova in 1609, the fruit of his long war with the orbit of Mars. No public-domain English translation exists, so the text stands here in Latin. Kepler worked from Tycho Brahe's superb records, the best naked-eye data ever gathered.

From those numbers Kepler forced out his first two laws of planet motion. Planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus. They also sweep equal areas in equal times. The laws broke the ancient rule that heavenly motion must be circular. Kepler told the story of his false starts in the book itself. It stands as a founding work of modern astronomy.
suess-face-of-earth-vol4-sollas-1909:
Volume 4 of Sollas's translation of Suess's Face of the Earth appeared in 1909. Eduard Suess turned to the Americas and the Atlantic in this volume of his global synthesis. The two American continents, north and south, get the same connected treatment he gave Asia.

Suess compared the Appalachians, Rockies, and Andes as parts of one crustal story, and he weighed the Atlantic's coasts and islands against each other. Matching rocks and fossils across the Atlantic fed his picture of former land links. Later plate tectonics explained those matches by moving continents instead. The volume is a prime record of how geology reasoned about the Americas and the Atlantic before that revolution came.
lister-collected-papers-vol1-1909:
Joseph Lister was a British surgeon who changed hospital care by fighting wound infection. He built on Pasteur's germ theory and began treating wounds with carbolic acid in the 1860s. His key papers were gathered after his death, and this first collected volume appeared in 1909.

The papers set out the antiseptic principle: kill germs in and around a wound, and patients stop dying of hospital gangrene. Lister reports operations, compares results before and after his method, and answers his critics. Death rates in his wards fell sharply. These writings mark the start of safe modern surgery.
lister-collected-papers-vol2-1909:
Joseph Lister, the British surgeon behind antiseptic surgery, published research across a long career. His collected papers were issued in two volumes in 1909. This second volume holds his later scientific work rather than the first antiseptic reports.

The papers study inflammation, the clotting of blood, and related questions in surgery and physiology. Lister describes experiments on animals and patients, and he refines the methods behind his wound care. Readers can watch a careful scientist test each claim step by step. Together with volume one, the set records how modern surgery was built, step by tested step, over one working lifetime.
pound-exultations-1909:
Ezra Pound, a young American poet in London, published Exultations in 1909. It was his third small book in little more than a year. Pound was teaching himself poetry by raiding the past, and this collection leans hard toward the medieval troubadours of Provence.

The poems include translations and imitations of troubadour songs, full of spring mornings, distant ladies, and formal praise. Early original lyrics stand beside them, already showing Pound's drive toward exact, musical speech. The medievalist and the modernist in Pound are both visible here, side by side. Exultations is a workshop book: readers can watch a revolutionary poet gathering his tools from a thousand years of verse.
pound-personae-1909:
Ezra Pound published Personae in London in 1909, his first substantial collection and his bid for poetic mastery. The title means masks in Latin, and Pound explained that each poem speaks through an adopted character or voice. He was twenty-three, freshly arrived from America, and determined to remake English poetry.

The poems move from troubadour translations to dramatic monologues and sharp lyrics. Pound tries on Provençal singers, Italian courtiers, and his own brash modern self. The technique is already dazzling, though the great Imagist manifestos still lay ahead. Critics took notice of the young American at once. Personae is the root from which Imagism and much of modern poetry grew.
kuprin-yama-1909:
Yama, also called The Pit, is Alexander Kuprin's novel of life in a brothel district of a southern Russian city. Kuprin published the first part in 1909, and Bernard Guilbert Guerney translated the book into English in 1922. Kuprin called it the first and last honest book on its subject.

Inside the houses of Yama, Kuprin follows the women, their keepers, their clients, and the students who debate their fate. He shows routine, humor, cruelty, and sudden violence without flinching. The book was banned in places, devoured everywhere, and argued over for years. Kuprin meant it as protest, not titillation, and its frankness still startles.
arabian-nights-burton-1885-vol-09:
Volume nine of Burton's Thousand Nights and a Night appeared in 1885, the penultimate book of the main set. Shahrazad's store seems endless even as its appointed end draws near. Kings in her tales keep meeting clever wives, lost sons, and fortunes reversed in a single night.

Burton, nearing his own finish line, still refuses every shortcut in the text. His renderings of verse stay verse, and his notes stay frank about manners and belief. The Gutenberg text of this volume is ebook 55587, set apart from its neighbors in numbering. That quirk aside, the volume matches the rest in dress. One volume more completes Shahrazad's bargain in the main series.
ocean-of-story-kathasaritsagara-tawney-1:
Volume nine of Penzer's Ocean of Story, issued from 1924, brings Tawney's Kathasaritsagara within reach of its close. Somadeva's ocean begins to gather its streams: the hero's long foretold destiny as emperor of the Vidyadharas stands near. Yet the tales refuse to thin out, and fresh wonders crowd the road to the throne.

Penzer's notes here lean on Indian custom, ritual, and law to gloss the tales' assumptions. Tawney translated with a schoolmaster's clarity, scene by scene, across thousands of verses. The Penzer edition remains the form in which English reads the whole Ocean. Volume nine is the last deep water before the shore. Its stories show no wear from the long voyage.
marett-threshold-of-religion-1909:
R. R. Marett published The Threshold of Religion at London in 1909, with Methuen. Marett, an Oxford anthropologist, challenged E. B. Tylor's famous claim that religion began in animism, the belief in spirits. He argued that something earlier and simpler stands at the threshold: awe before a vague, potent force like the mana of Pacific belief.

Taboo, dance, and ritual feeling, on his account, precede any doctrine of souls. The book founded the mana-taboo school in the early anthropology of religion. Marett writes with unusual grace for a theorist, and his examples range worldwide. Later scholars revised his scheme, yet his question still organizes the field. What comes first in religion, belief or feeling, is his lasting problem.
zohar-de-pauly-french-vol-4-1909:
Tome four of Jean de Pauly's French Zohar appeared in 1909. The Zohar, the Book of Splendor, is the great Aramaic commentary at the heart of the Kabbalah, framed as the teaching of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai. De Pauly gave the entire work in French between 1906 and 1911, the only complete public domain version.

The commentary moves through the Torah portion by portion. In each verse it finds the play of the sefirot. It tells of the wounds and healing of the Shekhinah, the presence of God in exile. Stories of the companions break the doctrine with sudden light. De Pauly's notes help the French reader through the symbols. The set advances here toward its close.
zohar-de-pauly-french-vol-5-1909:
The fifth tome of Jean de Pauly's Zohar also dates to 1909, as the translator pressed toward the end of his great task. The Zohar, the Book of Splendor, is the core book of Jewish mysticism, an Aramaic midrash on the Torah from the circle of Moses de Leon. De Pauly's French, in six tomes, is the only complete version in the public domain.

Portion by portion, the companions of Rabbi Shimon draw out the hidden life of God. They show the sefirot in their dance and the soul in its exile. Prayer becomes the repair of the worlds. Fierce debates and tender tales share the pages. De Pauly keeps the whole vast work in one steady French voice. One tome remains.
scheible-das-kloster-vol09:
In 1848 Johann Scheible published band nine of Das Kloster, with cells thirty-three through thirty-six. Nine bands in, his cloister held more rescued print than any rival project of the age. The German reading public for old magic, story, and charm had found its supplier.

Grimoires stand thick in this band, and Faust books and Höllenzwänge hold their usual dark corner. Folk charms, some only lines long, are printed with the same care as the great spell books. Chapbooks round out the stock with tales meant for winter nights. Band nine proves the set never coasted: the flow of rare texts stayed strong to the end.
saint-simon-memoirs-wormeley-vol-1-1909:
Louis de Rouvroy, duc de Saint-Simon, kept notes on the court of Louis XIV for thirty years. His years at Versailles ran from 1691 to 1723. The Mémoires were first published in 1829, long after his death. Volume one here opens Katharine Prescott Wormeley's English translation. Her version, made in 1899 to 1901, was printed in 1909 in four volumes.

Saint-Simon watched Versailles with a hawk's eye for rank, slight, and ambition. His pages swarm with dukes, ministers, mistresses, and spies, each drawn in a few unforgettable strokes. No other memoirist shows the Sun King's court from inside with such malice and brilliance. Volume one admits the reader to that gilded, dangerous world.
saint-simon-memoirs-wormeley-vol-2-1909:
Volume two of Wormeley's Saint-Simon continues the Mémoires of the duc de Saint-Simon in English. Saint-Simon wrote his memoirs from life at Versailles between 1691 and 1723, and they were first published in 1829. Wormeley's translation, made in 1899 to 1901 and printed in 1909, fills four volumes.

The court of Louis XIV fills these pages in all its ceremony and cruelty. Saint-Simon, a proud duke obsessed with rank, records every promotion, disgrace, and whisper of the palace. His portraits are so sharp that their subjects' descendants still wince. Historians treat the memoirs as a peerless source on the reign. Volume two keeps the court dancing under his merciless eye.
saint-simon-memoirs-wormeley-vol-3-1909:
Saint-Simon's Mémoires reach volume three in Katharine Prescott Wormeley's translation, the English set of 1899 to 1901, printed in 1909. Louis de Rouvroy, duc de Saint-Simon, composed his vast memoir from the years 1691 to 1723 at the court of France. Publication waited until 1829, when the book burst on a world that thought it knew Versailles.

Volume three holds more of the court's daily war of precedence, favor, and revenge. Saint-Simon hated the king's ministers and bastards, loved the old nobility, and wrote both loves and hatreds at full heat. The result is the greatest memoir of the age, half history and half settled scores. Its people live.
saint-simon-memoirs-wormeley-vol-4-1909:
Volume four completes Wormeley's English Saint-Simon, the translation of 1899 to 1901 printed in 1909. The duc de Saint-Simon's Mémoires, written from 1691 to 1723 and first published in 1829, close with the death of Louis XIV and the years that followed. Four volumes hold the English set entire.

The final volume keeps Saint-Simon's voice at full pitch: proud, funny, vindictive, and endlessly observant. His court portraits, from king to footman, form a whole society preserved in amber. Later writers from Proust onward have fed on these pages. To finish volume four is to leave Versailles at last, having seen it through the sharpest eyes in France.
berkeley-new-theory-vision-1709:
George Berkeley, a young Irish scholar, published An Essay Towards a New Theory of Vision in 1709. It was his first major work, written when he was only twenty-four. The question sounds simple: how do we see distance, size, and place? Berkeley's answer upset the settled teaching of his day.

He argues that distance, magnitude, and situation are not seen at all, in the strict sense. The eye gives us light and color; touch and habit teach us what those signs mean. Sight, for Berkeley, works like a language learned in childhood. The essay opened his path to immaterialism, the claim that being means being perceived. Its clarity still startles.
eucken-problem-human-life-1909:
Great thinkers from Plato onward have each formed a view of what human life is and should be. Rudolf Eucken gathered those views in Lebensanschauungen grosser Denker, a German survey of life views held by major minds. W. S. Hough and W. R. Boyce Gibson translated the work into English in 1909.

Eucken walks through the answers given across the ages, from Greek thought to his own century. He compares each view, notes what it grasps and what it misses, and builds toward his own position. The survey shows how one deep question kept changing shape. It also gives readers a guided tour of Western thought.
eucken-life-spirit-1909:
Philosophy itself is the problem at the heart of Rudolf Eucken's introduction, first printed in German and Englished by F. L. Pogson in 1909. Eucken refuses to treat philosophy as a fixed set of facts to hand over. Instead he presents it as work the human spirit must keep doing.

Across a few clear leading lines, he traces how that work went on through the centuries. Doubt and conflict mark the path, since spiritual life rests on no safe, given base. The book asks readers to take part in the search themselves. It served many newcomers as their first door into Eucken's thought.
kropotkin-great-french-revolution-dryhur:
Peter Kropotkin told the French Revolution from below in his history of 1789 to 1793. N. F. Dryhurst translated the work for Heinemann in 1909. The full English text runs to sixty eight chapters. Kings and assemblies share the stage with the Paris sections and village communes.

Peasant risings against feudal dues drive much of Kropotkin's story. He argues that common people, not leaders, made the Revolution's real gains. His anarchist sympathy shapes the telling without hiding the facts he gathered. The work rests on years in French archives. It remains a standard anarchist history of the event. Readers get the Revolution as a people's movement.
hobson-industrial-system-1909:
In The Industrial System of 1909, Hobson asks who earns income and who merely receives it. Rent and monopoly profits stand at the center of his inquiry. Some income pays for real work and risk, in his terms earned. Other income flows from owning scarce ground or holding a corner on a market.

Hobson calls that second kind unearned and asks how society should treat it. His ethics of distribution favor taxing the unearned share for public good. The book extends his underconsumptionist economics into moral territory. Reformers of his day quoted it often. It shows British liberal economics turning toward welfare questions. The argument remains clear and orderly.
spr-proceedings-vol21-1908-1909:
Parts fifty four, fifty five, and fifty six fill volume twenty one, for 1908 and 1909. The SPR enters its late Edwardian phase with new cases and old questions. Telepathy experiments run beside reports of hauntings and crisis apparitions. Trance mediumship still leads, with Piper's sittings drawing the closest study.

New mediums of the period, Thompson among the names in the files, get their hearings. The society prints failures of evidence as faithfully as successes. Volume twenty one keeps the central archive growing toward its 1930 horizon. Its reports fed books on survival for decades. Readers find the debate's texture here: careful, curious, unconvinced, unbowed.
corneille-polyeucte-constable-1909:
An Armenian Christian faces a pagan court in Corneille's Polyeucte, given here in Thomas Constable's Harvard Classics translation. Polyeuctus embraces the faith and smashes the idols, knowing the price is death. His wife Pauline, torn between her father, her old love, and her husband's God, carries the play's heart.

French classical tragedy reaches its religious summit in this drama of conversion and sacrifice. Duty and grace argue in high, ordered verse, as Corneille loved to stage them. The translation joins the library's Le Cid, letting English readers meet both faces of France's first great tragedian.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol09:
Liverpool issued Volume IX of the Journal of Discourses in 1862, while war tore at the nation the Saints had left behind. Brigham Young, his counsellors, and the Twelve speak in these pages, their sermons preserved by shorthand reporters. The church in Utah watched the conflict from its mountain distance.

Pulpit counsel here joins doctrine to the duties of a people building Zion in wartime's shadow. The printed sermons let scattered Saints share one teaching voice. Volume IX carries the year-by-year doctrinal record forward, part of a set prized for its closeness to the living speakers.
kawaguchi-three-years-in-tibet-1909:
Ekai Kawaguchi lived in Tibet disguised as a Chinese pilgrim, and Three Years in Tibet, from 1909, tells how he did it. Kawaguchi, a Japanese Zen monk seeking true texts of his faith, spent 1897 to 1903 reaching Lhasa and studying in its great monasteries. Detection meant death, and his road ran through years of cold, hunger, and fear.

His account, the first by a Japanese traveler, shows daily life in the closed capital as few books ever have. Temples, markets, medicine, and monks all pass under his patient, observant eye along the way. The narrative stands as a primary witness to the old Lhasa on the edge of change.
everyman-miracle-plays-rhys-1909:
Death summons Everyman, and every friend deserts him but Good Deeds, in the morality play printed with eight miracle plays in Ernest Rhys's 1909 edition. The Summoning of Everyman, from about 1500, stands as the supreme English morality play. Fellowship, Kindred, and Goods all refuse the road; only deeds walk with a man to the grave.

The companion pieces include the Wakefield Second Shepherds' Play, with its stolen sheep hidden in a cradle, and the Harrowing of Hell. Rhys's Everyman's Library volume joins the solemn and the comic faces of medieval drama. Together they show how English towns once staged the whole story of salvation.
swanton-tlingit-myths-and-texts-1909:
John Reed Swanton recorded myths and texts among the Tlingit of southeastern Alaska for the Bureau of American Ethnology. This 1909 bulletin prints them in Tlingit with English translation. The stories came from Tlingit tellers who held them as clan property and history.

The Raven cycle leads the collection. Raven steals the sun, makes the tides, and tricks his way through the early world. Other texts cover crest stories tied to clan crests, shaman narratives, and accounts of spirits and the dead. Swanton's careful texts preserve both the language and the lore of the Tlingit. They remain basic sources for Northwest Coast study.
frazer-psyches-task-1909:
In this short 1909 discourse, Frazer turned from myth to society and asked an odd question: what good did superstition do? His answer was that taboo and magic, though false beliefs, built real institutions.

Frazer argues that fear of spirits strengthened early government, guarded private property, and protected marriage and human life. The taboos that hedged a chief made authority possible; those around women and the dead shaped social order. He calls superstition a false but useful servant of progress. The essay is Frazer at his most pointed, and it influenced debates about how customs hold societies together.
stein-three-lives-1909:
Three Lives, published in 1909 at her own expense, was Gertrude Stein's first book. It tells the lives of three working women in the fictional city of Bridgepoint: two German servants and one young black woman.

'The Good Anna' and 'The Gentle Lena' follow servant girls through work, love, and early death in plain, repeating sentences. 'Melanctha', the longest, follows a restless young woman through a doomed love, in prose that loops and circles like thought itself. Stein's cubist sentences begin here, simple words arranged until they shimmer. The book announced a writer unlike any other.
james-pluralistic-universe-1909:
A Pluralistic Universe collects the Hibbert Lectures James gave at Oxford in 1908, published in 1909, the year before his death. It is his last full statement in metaphysics, aimed against the absolute idealism then ruling Oxford and Harvard alike.

Against the monism that made reality one perfect block, James defends a pluralistic world: unfinished, growing, and held together by real connections and real gaps. He draws on Fechner and Bergson and on his own radical empiricism. The lectures are warm, witty, and combative. They close the career of America's most humane philosopher with a plea for an open universe.
croce-aesthetic-1909:
Aesthetic as Science of Expression and General Linguistic, published in English in 1909 in Douglas Ainslie's translation, is Croce's foundational work on art. It opens his Philosophy of Spirit, the system that made him Italy's leading philosopher.

Art, Croce argues, is intuition given expression: not copying nature, not decoration, but the mind's first form of knowledge. From that claim he rebuilds the history and theory of aesthetics, treating language and art as one activity. The book's learning is vast and its tone magisterial. It set the terms of Italian criticism for a generation and traveled worldwide.
croce-philosophy-practical-1909:
Philosophy of the Practical, published in English in 1909, is the second volume of Croce's Philosophy of Spirit. After art and expression comes action: this book treats the economic and the ethical as the two practical forms of the spirit.

Croce distinguishes useful action, aimed at single ends, from moral action, aimed at the universal good, and shows how each corrupts the other when confused. Politics, law, and history are drawn into the scheme. The argument is abstract, but its stakes are conduct itself. With this volume, Croce's system covered both knowing and doing in one design.
plos-pone-0003409:
Katy Milne and colleagues looked at immune attack in ovarian cancer for this 2008 paper. Tumors filled with CD8 T cells tend to grow more slowly. Many patients also make antibodies against tumor proteins on their own. The team asked how those two responses relate in epithelial ovarian cancer.

They focused on antibodies against one tumor protein, NY-ESO-1. Patients with those antibodies also had strong T cell presence in tumors. The two arms of immunity seemed to answer the same tumor flag. That link supports efforts to treat this cancer through the immune system.
plos-pone-0003509:
Francisco J. Quintana, Aderet Solomon, and Irun R. Cohen studied how B cells switch antibody types in 2008. B cells weigh antigen signals from their own receptor plus help signals. Help can come from cytokines or from other cells. Toll-like receptors add another form of co-stimulation.

The team examined antibody IgG3 made against LPS, a bacterial surface molecule. Toll-like receptor 4 supplied a needed co-signal for that production. Two keys together license a specific antibody response. The finding shows how danger signals shape antibody choice. Antibody class choice decides how well a response clears each kind of germ.
plos-pone-0003609:
Yi-Hsiu Chen and co-authors studied gene control in a gut parasite in this 2008 paper. Giardia lamblia forms a cyst wall to survive outside its host. Three cyst wall protein genes switch on strongly during encystation. How those genes are governed was little known.

A factor called UPF1 regulates the cyst wall protein transcripts. UPF1 is conserved across life as part of nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. That system normally destroys faulty messages. Here it helps time the parasite's infectious transformation into a cyst. Giardia is a common cause of diarrhea in travelers and children worldwide.
plos-pone-0003709:
Yuko Seko, Noriyuki Azuma, Yoriko Takahashi, and colleagues published this eye study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The sclera is the tough white coat that holds and protects the eyeball. It does not itself take part in seeing, yet its diseases are hard to cure. The team studied its makeup across species.

They found the human sclera keeps traits in common with cartilage throughout evolution. That kinship reframes the white of the eye as a cartilage-like tissue. It also hints at new angles for treating scleritis, perforation, and the extreme nearsightedness tied to scleral change.
plos-pone-0003809:
Thomas G. Paulson, Patricia C. Galipeau, Lianjun Xu, and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The tumor suppressor gene p16 is altered in many human cancers. Barrett's esophagus is a premalignant change in the food pipe, often from chronic reflux. How often p16 mutates there was much less known.

The team charted the spectrum of p16 mutations in Barrett's tissue. They set those point changes beside other p16 damage known from cancers. The pattern helps mark the genetic road from a reflux-damaged esophagus toward cancer, and where checks might catch it early.
plos-pone-0003909:
Henrick Horita, Arthur E. Frankel, and Andrew Thorburn studied a targeted toxin against leukemia in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns acute myeloid leukemia, a fast blood cancer. The disease brings about 13,410 new U.S. cases and 8,990 deaths a year, they note. A lab-built toxin, DT-GMCSF, had shown it can kill leukemia stem cells.

The authors asked how that toxin kills the cells it targets. They found it switches on two death paths, apoptosis and necroptosis. A toxin that kills by two routes may be harder for cancer to dodge. The result guides how such toxins might be paired with other drugs.
plos-pone-0004009:
Yunzhao R. Ren, Fan Pan, Suhel Parvez, and co-authors tested an old drug on an immune channel in 2008. The Kv1.3 potassium channel matters in memory T cells. It is implicated in multiple sclerosis, psoriasis, and type 1 diabetes. Many groups have built blockers for that channel.

Their PLOS ONE article reports clofazimine blocks Kv1.3 in T lymphocytes. It does so by disturbing calcium oscillations inside the cells. Clofazimine is a known drug long used against leprosy. A second use in immune disease could speed new treatments. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004109:
Kira Foygel, Bokyung Choi, Sunny Jun, and co-authors studied a stem cell factor in early embryos in 2008. Oct4 is a master regulator of embryonic stem cell pluripotency. It is also highly expressed at the one- to two-cell embryo stage. The early embryo's gene network was far less known than the stem cell one.

Their PLOS ONE article reports a novel, critical role for Oct4. It regulates the maternal-to-embryonic transition in development. That handover switches control from mother's RNA to the embryo's genome. Oct4 thus bridges the stem cell and embryo gene programs. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004209:
Nathalie Mandairon and colleagues published this smell study in PLOS ONE in 2009. In humans, how pleasant an odor seems shapes social relations and food intake. Smells attract or repel according to their hedonic value, and these preferences shift with experience and learning.

The team asked whether mice share human olfactory preferences, judging the same odors as pleasant or unpleasant. A match between species would mean preferences are built into the nose, not just learned. The comparison matters for using mice to study a sense that, in humans, is deeply emotional.
plos-pone-0004309:
Andrzej Slominski and colleagues published this steroid study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The enzyme P450scc transforms 7-dehydrocholesterol, the skin's vitamin D precursor, into 7-dehydropregnenolone in the test tube. Whether living tissue performs the same chemistry was the open question.

The team studied adrenal glands from rats, pigs, rabbits, and dogs outside the body. They report rapid, time- and dose-dependent metabolism of 7-dehydrocholesterol into steroidal 5,7-dienes. They also discuss what this pathway implies for the skin, where the starting compound is plentiful and sunlight adds energy. The work was done on glands from four species, which makes the shared result stronger.
plos-pone-0004409: In 2009, Belin, Kaya, and Duisit found vitamin C starving tumors. Ascorbic acid slowed tumor growth by shutting down cell-cycle genes. The vitamin silenced key growth genes. The finding reframes vitamin C in cancer research. The high dose made the difference.
plos-pone-0004509: In 2009, a team brewed tricky cell antennas in vats. Big batches of lab-made human scent receptors were cleaned up. The tough antenna proteins were coaxed soluble. The method now serves drug hunt pipelines. The receptors sit in greasy cell walls.
plos-pone-0004609: In 2009, Capellini, McNamara, and Preston asked whether sleep cements memories. Sleep's role in memory consolidation was tested across mammals. The big comparative test found weak support overall. The finding challenges the sleep-is-for-brain view head-on. The true purpose stays obscure.
plos-pone-0004709: In 2009, Stauch, Dernier, and Sarmiento Marchese found transplant drugs hitting natural killers hard. Natural killer cells were targeted by rabbit antithymocyte globulin and Campath-1H. The effects looked similar indeed. The study informs transplant care today. The strategies deplete T cells.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-09:
Quebec in the single year 1636 is the focus of Volume 9, from 1897. By then the young colony on the St. Lawrence was taking root. Thwaites prints the year's reports as the mission kept steady annual records of its work.

Schools open, a hospital rises, and church life gains a firm frame. Priests count converts, note deaths, and plan the next season's work. Settlers and Native guests move through the small town each day. Growth looks modest, yet the writers build as if for ages. The volume shows how a colony of faith was planted, year by careful year.
journal-of-discourses-vol-09:
War's middle years fill Volume Nine of the Journal, issued in 1862. The Saints prosper in their valleys while the Union fights for life. Young presses self-sufficiency in nearly every discourse of this span.

Home industry, grain reserves, and new settlements lead his public counsel. Converts keep gathering from Europe to swell the kingdom's towns. The discourses build Zion's workshops as Babylon tears itself apart. That sharp contrast gives Mormon Utah its odd, proud edge here. Faith, thrift, and defiance blend in the Tabernacle's weekly public voice. The volume shows prosperity preached as proof of divine favor.
bernard-sermons-advent-christmas-1909:
John Hedley translated Bernard's sermons for Advent and Christmas into English in 1909. Bernard preached these sermons to his monks at Clairvaux in the twelfth century, marking the opening weeks of the church year. Advent, the season of waiting for Christ's coming, drew some of his most tender preaching.

The sermons treat Christ's coming in three ways: in history at Bethlehem, in the soul by grace, and in glory at the end. Bernard moves between close reading of Scripture and warm address to his hearers. His honeyed style, which earned him the name mellifluous doctor, is at its gentlest here. Hedley's translation gave English readers the devotional Bernard, the preacher of longing and joy, rather than the controversialist of the letters.
hobson-crisis-of-liberalism-1909:
John Hobson published The Crisis of Liberalism in 1909, as Britain fought over the People's Budget and the power of the House of Lords. Hobson was the leading economic writer of the New Liberalism, the movement that was remaking the Liberal Party. The book gathers his case against the old creed of laissez-faire, the doctrine that the state should leave the economy alone.

Hobson argues that poverty and monopoly are not natural facts but products of a system the state may lawfully change. He calls for public action on housing, wages, and the taxation of unearned gains. The essays gave British progressivism its economic conscience in plain, forceful prose. Read today, the book marks the moment when British liberalism turned toward the welfare state.
monro-digest-justinian-vol2-1909:
Monro's English Digest of Justinian reached a second volume in 1909. The Digest itself, Justinian's sixth-century gathering of Roman jurists, runs to fifty books, so translation was a long labor. Monro, a fellow of a Cambridge college, worked through it with the patience of a practicing lawyer.

Volume 2 continues through the early books of the Digest, where the jurists treat actions, contracts in their first forms, and the protection of property. The decisions are concrete: real disputes about sales, loans, and guardianship, answered in a few exact lines. Readers meet Roman law as working law, not as marble. The classical law of Rome becomes available book by book to the English bar and to students who lack Latin. Monro's two volumes remain a standard doorway into the Digest.
